name: OpenSSL (Keccak-1600 x86_64 assembly, SHA3-256)
baseline: Keccak Code Package (XKCP) x86_64 assembly Keccak-f[1600] module; also compiler-generated C Keccak (gcc 5.x/4.x/3.x)
workload: Cycles per processed byte on a large message for SHA3-256 (rate r=1088) using OpenSSL's crypto/sha/asm/keccak1600-x86_64.pl, on twelve x86 CPU families.
claimed_speedup: Author comment in the file header (June 2017): 'How does it compare to x86_64 assembly module in Keccak Code Package? Depending on processor it's either as fast or faster by up to 15%'. Same header: improvement over compiler-generated code 'most common coefficient is 15% in comparison to gcc-5.x, 50% for gcc-4.x, 90% for gcc-3.x'. Absolute figures (cycles/byte, SHA3-256): Haswell 9.6, Skylake 9.4, Ryzen 8.8, Core 2 12.9, Sandy Bridge 12.9, Bulldozer 16.5. No cycles-per-byte figure is given for the Keccak Code Package baseline.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the Keccak Code Package comparison; compiler-generated C baseline given only as gcc 5.x / 4.x / 3.x with no flags.
hardware: Table over P4, Core 2, Westmere, Sandy Bridge, Haswell, Skylake, Silvermont, Goldmont, VIA Nano, Sledgehammer, Bulldozer, Ryzen; no model numbers or clock speeds.
stars_or_usage: 30.9k stars; the default TLS/crypto library on most Linux distributions
tradeoffs: The claim covers one hand-written x86_64 Perl-generated assembly module (SHA-3/SHAKE permutation), not OpenSSL as a whole. Using it means linking OpenSSL (large, Apache-2.0) or extracting the cryptogams-licensed module (dual-licensed OpenSSL and CRYPTOGAMS per the file header). Other CPU architectures use other code paths.
caveats: Evidence is an author comment inside a source header dated June 2017, not a published benchmark: the Keccak Code Package figures are not given, no compiler flags, CPU models, clock speeds or benchmark harness are stated, and the Keccak Code Package (now XKCP) has been developed since. The 'faster by up to 15%' range includes 'as fast', so on some CPUs the result is a tie. OpenSSL is itself the incumbent baseline for most crypto in this catalog; no external benchmark showing OpenSSL beating another named library was found in reachable sources (wolfSSL and RTI pages were unreachable). Other in-source tables in the same repo compare OpenSSL assembly only against its own earlier code or gcc-compiled C (chacha-x86_64.pl, ghash-x86_64.pl, rsaz-avx2.pl, ecp_nistz256-x86_64.pl); CHANGES.md reports 1.6x to 4.5x for the new SHA-512 ISA-extension path on an Intel Core Ultra 5 238V, which is OpenSSL against its own previous code path.

name: xxhash_cpp
baseline: MurmurHash3a (README table also lists CityHash64, FNV, CRC32, MD5-32, SHA1-32); std::hash and djb2 are not measured
workload: SMHasher speed test of the upstream xxHash C library, reproduced in the README of this C++17 port (the port itself is not measured).
claimed_speedup: README table: xxHash 5.4 GB/s vs MurmurHash 3a 2.7 GB/s, CityHash64 1.05 GB/s, FNV 0.55 GB/s, CRC32 0.43 GB/s, MD5-32 0.33 GB/s, SHA1-32 0.28 GB/s (about 2.0x over MurmurHash 3a, derived from page data). Second table: XXH64 13.8 GB/s and XXH32 6.8 GB/s on 64-bit, 1.9 GB/s and 6.0 GB/s on 32-bit.
compiler_and_flags: First table: Visual C++ 2010, Windows 7 32-bit; second table: GCC 4.8.2, Linux Mint 64-bit; flags not stated.
hardware: First table: Core 2 Duo @ 3 GHz; second table: Core i5-3340M @ 2.7 GHz.
tradeoffs: Single standalone header (xxhash.hpp), C++17, template API for 32 and 64 bit variants with overloads for vector, string, array, iterators and streaming state; static linking only; build macros for endianness and unaligned reads; arm64 builds use sse2neon.
caveats: The numbers measure upstream xxHash (C reference, 2012-era SMHasher runs), copied into this port's README, not the port: no benchmark code or numbers for xxhash_cpp itself exist in the repo, and none compare it against the C implementation or std::hash. Hardware and compilers are very old. Open issue #47 (opened 2026-08-26) is titled 'xxhash3_impl declared as XXH_NO_INLINE is not a faithful port of the original' (title only read). Likely a port/duplicate of the existing xxHash entry.
